public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Bugeaud Collection of Conjectures and Open Questions: Mahler's Z-numbers

See also FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/Mahler32.lean.

*References:*
  - [Bug12] Bugeaud, Yann. "Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation."
    Vol. 193. Cambridge University Press, 2012. Chapter 10.
  - [Mah68] Mahler, Kurt. "An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2."
    Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 8.2 (1968): 313-321.
  - [FLP95] Flatto, Leopold, Jeffrey C. Lagarias, and Andrew D. Pollington.
    "On the range of fractional parts $\{\xi(p/q)^n\}$."
    Acta Arithmetica 70.2 (1995): 125-147.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Bugeaud09

/--
Problem 10.9. There are no real numbers $\xi$ such that $0 \le \{\xi (3/2)^n\} < 1/2$
for every positive integer $n$, i.e. no Z-number exists. Posed by Mahler [Mah68].
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem problem_10_9 : type_of% Mahler32.mahler_conjecture := by
  sorry

/--
Sanity check: `1` is not a Z-number, since for `n = 1` we have
$\{1 \cdot (3/2)^1\} = \{3/2\} = 1/2 \not< 1/2$.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isZNumber_one : ¬ IsZNumber 1 := by
  rintro ⟨-, h⟩
  have h1 := h 1 le_rfl
  rw [pow_one, one_mul] at h1
  have hfr : Int.fract (3 / 2 : ℝ) = 1 / 2 := by rw [Int.fract]; norm_num [Int.floor_eq_iff]
  rw [hfr] at h1
  exact lt_irrefl _ h1

/--
Mahler [Mah68] proved that the set of Z-numbers has Lebesgue measure zero.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem problem_10_9.variants.measure_zero :
    MeasureTheory.volume {ξ : ℝ | IsZNumber ξ} = 0 := by
  sorry

/--
Flatto, Lagarias, and Pollington [FLP95] proved that the set of Z-numbers has
Hausdorff dimension strictly less than $1$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem problem_10_9.variants.dimH_lt_one :
    dimH {ξ : ℝ | IsZNumber ξ} < 1 := by
  sorry

end Bugeaud09

findings.description: The docstring says there are no real numbers ξ satisfying the displayed fractional-part inequalities, but omits ξ > 0. Taken literally, this is false: ξ = 0 satisfies every displayed inequality. The Lean statement correctly includes positivity through IsZNumber, so this is a prose-only defect, not a misformalization of the theorem.
findings.source_evidence: Mahler (1968), p. 313, begins 'Let α be an arbitrary positive number' before defining Z-numbers. Bugeaud (2012), Definition 3.2, p. 50, likewise says 'A positive real number ξ is a Z-number'. The abbreviated wording of Problem 10.9 itself also omits this restriction. Sources: https://doi.org/10.1017/S1446788700005371 and Bugeaud's Google Books previews, https://books.google.com/books?id=NeEpoAf7k0IC&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Mahler .
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to 'There are no positive real numbers ξ such that ...'. Leave the Lean statement unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The imported IsZNumber checks exponents n ≥ 1, whereas Mahler's original definition and Bugeaud's Definition 3.2 check n ≥ 0. This does not change the nonexistence conjecture.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let Z₀(x) mean x > 0 and fract(x(3/2)^n) < 1/2 for every n ≥ 0. Then IsZNumber x ↔ Z₀((3/2)x), by replacing n with n+1. Multiplication by 3/2 is a bijection on the positive reals, so universal nonexistence is equivalent under the two conventions. These equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/equivalences.lean without using either conjecture.

reformulations.difference: The Lean null-set statement uses the n ≥ 1 convention, while the set in Mahler's paper uses n ≥ 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Writing S₀ for Mahler's set and S₁ for the Lean set, S₁ = (x ↦ (3/2)x)⁻¹(S₀). Consequently volume(S₁) = (2/3) volume(S₀), so either set has measure zero exactly when the other does. The set identity and the measure-zero biconditional were proved in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The Lean Hausdorff-dimension statement uses the n ≥ 1 convention, while FLP's Z₃/₂(0,1/2) uses n ≥ 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The two sets are related by the invertible dilation x ↦ (3/2)x. Hausdorff dimension is invariant under this bi-Lipschitz map. Equality of their Hausdorff dimensions, and hence equivalence of the bounds dimH < 1, were proved in Lean.

sources_consulted: Yann Bugeaud, Distribution Modulo One and Diophantine Approximation (2012), Chapter 10 introduction: https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139017732.012 ; Problem 10.9, p. 215, via https://books.google.com/books?vid=ISBN9780521111690&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=%2210.9%22 .

Bugeaud (2012), Definition 3.2, p. 50, via Google Books search previews: https://books.google.com/books?id=NeEpoAf7k0IC&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=Mahler and https://books.google.com/books?id=NeEpoAf7k0IC&jscmd=SearchWithinVolume2&q=%22Z-number%22 .

Kurt Mahler, 'An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2', Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 8 (1968), 313–321, especially equation (1) and §3, equation (11): https://doi.org/10.1017/S1446788700005371 .

Leopold Flatto, Jeffrey C. Lagarias and Andrew D. Pollington, 'On the range of fractional parts {ξ(p/q)^n}', Acta Arithmetica 70 (1995), 125–147, especially pp. 126–127 and Theorem 1.1: https://www.impan.pl/shop/publication/transaction/download/product/108521?download.pdf .
review.notes: All four Lean statements checked out mathematically. Mahler's §3 and FLP Theorem 1.1 (specialized to p=3, q=2, s=0, t=1/2) establish countability, which supports both solved variants; indeed their sets have Hausdorff dimension zero. The test theorem has no sorry dependency. Boundary tests and equivalence proofs compiled in /workspace/review/. Cambridge's full Chapter 10 PDF was unavailable; its introduction and Google Books previews were checked alongside the complete cited papers.
